paragraphs: In autumn, the wind along the Huai River always freshened after sunset. People on its banks gradually grew used to hearing oars in the night.

Sometimes there were only one or two strokes, like a fish’s tail striking the surface. Sometimes a stifled sob carried through the wind, so faint beyond several beds of reeds that no one could tell whether it came from a person or a bird. Qin soldiers on patrol boats pursued with torches and found only darkness at first, then face after wet face.

The first group was nine people carrying bedding, an earthenware pot, and half a sack of rice. They claimed to be coming to the northern bank to gather herbs. Three days later another twenty-three crossed, among them two former Jin soldiers. Another ten days passed and a boat carrying refugees capsized midstream; only eleven were rescued. One woman clung so fiercely to a wooden chest that she would not release it even after being hauled aboard. When it was opened, all it contained was a roll of family genealogy and a door key so rusty it would scarcely turn.
The clerk at the ferry asked whether she had anything valuable. “The key,” she answered.
“Your door is still on the southern bank. What use have you for it?”
“I cannot go back.” She lowered her head and wiped the chest. “But the door is still there.”

More than three hundred people were detained at several checkpoints. Army headquarters said they were subjects of Jin and belonged in the hands of frontier troops. The counties said that, once ashore, they had to be fed. The household office searched its old registers and found no category in which to put them. Someone entered them provisionally as “surrendered households,” whereupon a scholar from Jiangnan struck the table and shouted, “No city has fallen, no army has been defeated. To whom have I surrendered?”
The junior clerk lost his temper too. “If you have not surrendered, why cross the river?”

The man’s face reddened. His lips moved twice, but no words came. He had once despised the northern people’s foreign dress; before crossing, however, he had wrapped his father’s inkstone in three layers of cloth and carried it eighty li on his back. His wife and children were waiting beside him for their porridge.

The dispute at the ferry was still unsettled in late autumn. At last the Shouchun military headquarters issued a temporary order: people whose origins could not be verified were to remain in custody; those whose cases stayed unclear might be returned after consultations with Jin officers. On the night the news reached the river, the wind was high. Yet a boat carrying a white lantern came openly from the southern bank.

A white cloth at the bow bore the character for mourning; beneath the lantern hung the silhouette of half a thin coffin. The boatman made no attempt to conceal his oars. Instead he beat a copper basin as he crossed, as though afraid the people ashore would not hear him. A fast Jin boat came out in pursuit, and the Qin watch raised the alarm from the north. Before the horns had fallen silent on either bank, the larger boat was caught between them in midstream.

When Qin commandant Li Qian boarded, there was scarcely room to put a foot down. Seventeen children pressed around the cabin entrance in faded scholars' robes, their books and bamboo slips tied with hemp cord. Beside them lay farm tools, two torn mats, and earthen jars of dried provisions. A woman in mourning hemp sat before the coffin. She rose at the rattle of armor.
“I am Shen Lingyi, of Xuyi.”
“Who is in the coffin?”
“My late husband, Zhou Shu.”
“Which army did he serve in?”
“He was formerly magistrate of a county under Xuyi.”

Li Qian ordered the coffin inspected. When its lid was lifted, it held only an earthenware urn of ashes, a few rolls of old books, and an oil-stained official robe. Li Qian had just begun to relax when someone cried out at the stern. Patrolmen found two short knives and a bow beneath a straw mat, then dragged out three farm men whose palms were calloused from weapons. Next they discovered an oilcloth packet inside a young man’s blue-green robe. It contained detailed drawings of roads, canals, beacon towers, and grain depots.
Li Qian seized his sword hilt. “A fine funeral indeed! Military maps of Jin hidden beneath a coffin!”
The young man hurried to speak. “I brought the maps. My teacher’s widow knew nothing of them.”
“Your name?”
“Xu Cheng. I kept accounts for Magistrate Zhou.”
“Why carry military maps?”
“Turn them over.”

Li Qian flipped the sheets. On their backs, closely written entries recorded the fields of more than a hundred households: one man had borrowed two dou of millet and owed one mu of land after the spring harvest; another household had worked thirty days on the embankment yet still owed the same official rent as the year before. Several names circled in red were followed by the seal marks of a single estate.

Shen Lingyi hugged the urn close and at last spoke. “My husband was investigating the land registers after the floods. The fields drowned year after year. Estates lent grain in exchange for deeds, and the people lost their land while the county still demanded labor service. He tried to change that, so someone accused him of exchanging intelligence with Qin officials.”
Li Qian stared at her. “Did he?”

“He exchanged reports about the water,” said Xu Cheng. “It is the same river. If the sluices open on the north bank, the south floods. Unless both sides exchange warnings, people on both banks will die. Someone intercepted his letter, and he was arrested as a spy. He died on the road before he ever reached Jiankang.”

Li Qian looked down at the little urn. A swift boat from the southern bank was already approaching. A Jin commandant shouted across the water that the vessel carried criminals accused of stealing official documents, evading service, and killing or wounding government soldiers. By established practice they must be handed back. The farmers on deck grew agitated. Some swore they had killed no one; others said the pursuers had fired arrows first. Li Qian asked about the weapons his men had found. The knives were certainly old, but that alone did not establish the men’s innocence.
“Tow them to shore first,” he ordered. “Hold those carrying weapons separately. Give the children water.”
“You intend to hide Jin criminals?” the Jin commandant shouted angrily.

Li Qian would not debate the matter in midstream. When the boat reached the northern bank, the seventeen children were taken first to an empty granary, and the three farmers were detained separately at army headquarters. Shen Lingyi came last, holding the urn. As she crossed the threshold she stooped to move aside a splinter of bamboo, afraid a child might step on it and fall.

The next day local people gathered outside the ferry station. Feng Shun stood at their head holding his land deed and shouting loudly enough to be heard down the street. His son had died repairing the embankment the previous year, and the county had yet to deliver the wasteland promised in compensation. Hearing that the southern arrivals might be given fields, he had brought more than a dozen other households still waiting for their allotments to block the granary gate.

“If the government has grain, let it give it to those of us who repaired the northern embankment!” He slapped his deed. “My son died in the water, and I still have no field. Yet boatloads of pupils raised by rich southerners arrive and must be fed first?”
Shen Lingyi came out. “We have not asked for your land.”
“The moment you cross the river, you need grain and a roof. Where is the grain to come from? Where are the waste fields to come from?”

She opened her mouth, then realized she had no good answer. A thin child peered out behind her. “We study with our teacher’s wife,” he said. One of Feng Shun’s companions picked up a lump of mud and threw it against the doorframe. The child drew back with tears in his eyes. Shen Lingyi steadied the back of his neck, shut the door, and bolted it with trembling hands.

Commander Xue Zhi did not arrive until evening. He had defended this stretch of river for seven years, and old wounds ached when it rained. The grain office reported that the stores at the ferry could feed six hundred additional people for only twenty days. If another thousand arrived that winter, grain would have to be borrowed from Luoyang. Even wasteland cleared along the river might not yield a crop the next year.
“You have forty-seven people aboard that boat,” Xue Zhi asked Shen Lingyi. “Have you calculated how much they eat in a year?”
“No.”

“I have.” He spread open the grain accounts. “Your boat is not the only group I must feed. The Feng family, who helped repair last year’s embankment, is still waiting for its compensation. This year’s garrison soldiers have had their rations reduced too. If I keep every southerner, which Qin household should lose a shi of grain?”
Shen Lingyi studied the figures for a long time before speaking. “Then I ask you, General, to report the facts exactly as they stand.”

Xue Zhi had expected a plea for mercy. Instead she told him to record the grain, land, military risk and resentment of local people in full. Her husband had once written only of the suffering of the villagers, she said, and court officials accused him of concealing the true state of the waters. If Chang’an now heard only how pitiful her children were, it would forget Feng Shun’s son.

Xue Zhi looked at her without speaking. That night he wrote his report himself, adding one sentence at the end: “Those who come from the South cannot all be driven away; the old inhabitants of Qin cannot all be made to yield.”

When the military report reached the Secretariat in Chang’an, the ministers had already been arguing for days about next year’s grain taxes. The household office wanted to enter the southerners into Qin registers at once. Army headquarters proposed treating them provisionally as farming-garrison households. Some imperial clansmen urged closing the frontier and leaving Jiangnan to its own troubles. Fu Hong turned to the end of the report and found a thin ledger unlike any approved form, its edges stained with porridge. Beneath some names were entries no more precise than “one elderly person, two sick children.”
“What is this?”
“A junior clerk downstream altered an old military roll because he feared people would collect porridge twice.”
“How long has he kept it?”
“Since the first boats reached shore.”

Fu Hong read several pages. Beside one child’s name, someone had added in small characters: “Fever last night; sent for treatment.” He set the page before Fu Rong and asked which state’s accounts should bear those medical costs if the people were sent back.

Fu Rong did not answer the rhetorical question. He pushed another register of lands north of the Huai across the table. “How many people can the court sustain? Calculate that first. Families whose men died defending the embankment must not be left waiting.”

The finance official reported the grain available for autumn and winter. Fu Jian listened from beside the curtain and asked whether, if they admitted only a thousand people, ten thousand might arrive the next year. The official said yes, perhaps more. Fu Jian asked the assembly to stop for a moment, then said, “The children from that boat are already ashore. Who among you can guarantee that if we send them back, they will not be put to the sword?”
No one in the hall could give such a guarantee.

Fu Hong ordered the temporary ledgers from every ferry sent to the household office. For the time being, clerks were to enter names, places of origin, family members, possessions and any charges requiring investigation, without compelling the arrivals to change their formal allegiance immediately. When someone asked under what heading, he looked at the old ledger and replied, “Register them as resident guests for now.”
“And how long may a guest remain?”

“Let us provisionally set three years. Grain and land limits must be calculated separately. Those found with weapons are to be questioned under military law, but sick women and children must be treated first. Land already promised to residents must not be taken without compensation for the newcomers. If the counties north of the Huai have no room, settle people elsewhere and provide the first year’s grain from the central government. No single county must bear the whole burden.”

For several days afterward the Secretariat revised the draft again and again. Resident guests would not be subject to military service for three years; after receiving land they would pay rent on what was actually harvested. Those wishing to return south could apply to do so, and the word “guest” could not be used as a pretext for imprisonment. Nor could accusations of unpaid taxes or evaded labor under the southern government suffice, on the strength of one document from the opposite bank, to hand anyone over.

Cases involving concealed bows or knives, or spying on frontier defenses, would be investigated household by household; all forty-seven passengers would not be held guilty for one person’s act. Fu Rong insisted on adding that land promised to long-established local households could not be taken away, and Fu Hong agreed. On the last page, Fu Jian wrote a single character: “Trial.” The order would be applied for three months first, and the reports at its end must include mistaken accounts, disputed land and petitions of appeal.

A drafting official asked whether the decree should begin, “The people of the South, admiring Qin’s benevolent rule...” Fu Jian glanced at the porridge-stained ledger on his desk. “They are fleeing disaster, forced labor and lawsuits. They come for a mouthful of food. Why put words of loyal devotion into their mouths?”
The decree reached the northern bank of the Huai on the very morning Xue Zhi had fixed for the refugees' return.

The Jin boat from the south already lay midstream, and Qin soldiers were loosening the mooring ropes. Shen Lingyi held her husband’s urn to her breast. The children had put on their worn shoes. Several had agreed to jump into the river as soon as the boat cleared the barrier. Xue Zhi stood on the shore with a bitter taste in his mouth. He knew that if he defied the order on his own authority and Jin soldiers crossed on a pretext of provocation, he would bear the blame.

Hooves suddenly sounded from the north. An express rider fell with his saddle into the wet earth. Even as he scrambled upright, he held his sealed dispatch high. Xue Zhi broke the seal, read two pages, and turned to shout toward the river. “We are not handing them over. Their cases are not closed. We cannot.”
The Jin commandant was furious. “Does Qin intend to shelter criminals of Jin?”
“If they have killed or spied on military defenses, we shall investigate those charges ourselves. People who crossed the river to escape labor service cannot be bound and sent back for that alone.”

A swift current separated the soldiers on the two banks. Hands tightened on weapons, but neither side fired an arrow. After a long while the Jin boat turned around, its wake slapping the Qin landing stage.

Shen Lingyi did not kneel in thanks. She first asked what would become of Xu Cheng and the three farmers held separately. Xue Zhi said their cases would be investigated: if they had committed crimes, they would be punished, but without evidence they could not be detained as spies forever. She then asked whether the seventeen children might remain together. He replied that their family and teacher-pupil ties would be registered first, so that no child without a guardian would be scattered or lost.

Feng Shun was still waiting outside the camp gate with his deed. Xue Zhi showed him the new decree and pointed to the provision forbidding the seizure of promised local land. Feng Shun did not trust official papers. “Another trick to fool an old man,” he muttered. Xue Zhi did not demand gratitude. He ordered the chief clerk to post in public that month’s register of fields owed for embankment work, to be checked separately from the new guest register. Feng Shun put his deed back inside his robe. Before leaving, he glanced at Shen Lingyi and said nothing.

That night two iron cauldrons were set over fires in the abandoned granary. An old soldier brought in half a basket of firewood. His foot caught a fallen copy of the classics. Picking it up, he tried to read a line as he once had: “When a friend comes from afar...”
He could not remember the rest. The youngest child supplied it: “Is it not a joy?”
The old soldier chuckled and set down the wood. “You little masters remember better than I do.”

Shen Lingyi sat by the lamp, sewing new book satchels for the seventeen children. Her husband’s urn stood in a corner, covered by his old official robe. There were no ancestral graves here, no deed to a house, and the roof still let the wind through. She did not know whether another official would come to question them tomorrow. But the children could already read aloud by lamplight.

A few days later, the southern bank began stricter inspections of riverboats. Fewer crossed by day, but the oars did not fall silent at night. One winter morning a patrol dragged in a leaking little boat from midstream. Thirty-one people were packed into it, their padded coats frozen stiff. As soon as the bow touched the landing stage, they scrambled for the bank and nearly overturned the vessel. Xue Zhi hurried up, made them sit back down, ordered the physicians to bring hot water, and had a clerk open the resident-guest register.

As usual, the clerk began to ask where they came from. But Xue Zhi noticed an infant whose lips were turning blue. He hurriedly passed the baby to a physician. Standing on thin ice, water soaking through the soles of his boots, he called to the boat, “Who knows how to look after this child? Come here first. Stop pushing!”

The southern bank still showed fires through the mist; only one granary door was open on the northern shore. By afternoon several newly arrived households had yet to be registered when Feng Shun came again to the chief clerk with his deed: half a mu of the land promised him last year was still missing. Hearing the argument, Xue Zhi turned and shouted for someone to fetch the old county maps. There was no reason to make the old man come back empty-handed yet again.

The water whispered coldly against the wooden piles of the landing stage. Across the river, Jiangnan was still these people’s homeland; the northern shore beneath their feet was hardly a new home. Yet from that day onward the ferry had one more register, a room where a pot of medicine was kept warm, and a group of people still unsure how to live together. Whenever another boat came out on the river, someone raised a lantern toward that mass of black water.
